text: Chapter 3 covered crawlers, the Catalog, and ETL jobs — all of it assumes incoming data is shaped the way you expect. AWS Glue Data Quality is the piece that actually checks that assumption, with a real rule language purpose-built for it, rather than hand-rolled validation logic inside a Glue ETL script.

A DQDL document is a case-sensitive list named Rules, inside square brackets. IsComplete checks whether a column is ever null, IsUnique checks for repeated values, RowCount sanity-checks the row total, and ColumnValues and Completeness check a numeric range or a populated fraction. IsComplete and IsUnique already return true or false on their own — the others need an expression like greater-than or between to turn a value into a pass or fail.

This is the actual rule builder inside Glue Studio — eighteen rule types you can search and insert, with live validation. Here, a ColumnCorrelation rule is flagged with an error before the job ever runs, catching a mistake early instead of failing silently in production.

Multiple rules combine with and or or, each wrapped in parentheses. Here's the detail worth being precise about: by default, a composite rule evaluates each side independently across the entire column, then combines the two overall results — it does not check both conditions against the same row. And a with-threshold clause lets a rule pass if a set percentage of rows satisfy it, tolerating a small amount of real-world messiness instead of requiring everything to be perfect.

DQDL rules can run inside a Glue ETL job, through an Evaluate Data Quality node wired right into the job graph — shown here between two Data Catalog sources and their outputs, with the rule editor and a Helper panel of rule types open alongside it. This gets you the full feature set: dynamic rules comparing against historical metrics, labels, and row-level pass or fail results you can act on in the same job.

Rules can also attach directly to a table in the Data Catalog, with no custom ETL script required — simpler to set up, but dynamic rules, analyzers, and labels aren't supported there. For a quick standing check on a table, the Catalog option is the lower-effort choice. For a pipeline that needs to react to a specific failing row, the rules belong inside the ETL job.

That closes this chapter. You've gone from a table format that makes safe concurrent writes possible, to permissions fine-grained enough to hide a single column, to a rule language that checks whether the data flowing through all of it can actually be trusted.
